# Testing

Use only the rules that apply to the current consumer task.

## Contents

- [Keep consumer tests fast](#keep-consumer-tests-fast)
- [Separate reusable test helpers from library tests](#separate-reusable-test-helpers-from-library-tests)

## Keep consumer tests fast

Share one database container per test assembly, give every test or host a database of its own copied from a template that is migrated once, move a registered test TimeProvider instead of waiting, and run focused tests while building.

## Preferred approach

Start one database container per test assembly, not per test or test class. Use
an xUnit assembly fixture (`[assembly: AssemblyFixture(typeof(...))]` in xUnit
v3) that starts the container lazily, when a test first asks for a database, and
disposes it when the run ends; test classes and class fixtures receive it in
their constructor. A run without database tests then starts no container.
SPM-309's `SamplePostgreSqlServer` is the executable example.

Give every test, or every test host, a database of its own on that container, so
test classes run in parallel without sharing rows. Migrate a template database
once per run and copy it for each host: on PostgreSQL, close the template's
pooled connections, refuse new ones and create each database with
`CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE ...`, as `CreateMigratedDatabaseAsync` does. On SQL
Server, or wherever copying is not available, keep a small pool of migrated
databases and empty their tables when a test leases one, keeping the migration
history. A test that
proves the migrations themselves creates an empty database of its own.

Start a test host once per class fixture and share it between the tests of that
class. Build other expensive things, such as models, keys and seed data, once.
The NewHeap assistant's endpoints get their request delegates when the package is
built, so mapping the assistant adds a few milliseconds to a host start instead of
compiling every endpoint again; profile the rest of a slow host start first.

Register a test `TimeProvider` as the host's application clock, replacing any
earlier registration, and move it forward instead of waiting. NewHeap libraries
read the application's clock (a registered `TimeProvider`, otherwise the system
clock) for business deadlines: when a background operation becomes due
(`NotBefore`, retry backoff), how long a trigger debounces, the minute a schedule
tick belongs to and how long an approval lives. Leases, heartbeats and audit
timestamps keep the system clock, so moving the test clock forward never takes
work away from a running attempt. `SampleTestClock` adds a forward-only offset
to real time.

Wait for work through a signal, or poll a condition with a generous upper bound
that only matters when the test fails. Assert the outcome, not how long it took.

While building, run the focused test class
(`dotnet test --filter FullyQualifiedName~<Class>`). Run the complete suite, on
every provider the application supports, before merging.

## Avoid

- Starting a database container per test or per test class.
- Applying migrations per test or per host when a template copy or a reset of a
  migrated database would do.
- Sharing rows between test classes or depending on the order in which tests run.
- `Task.Delay` or `Thread.Sleep` as a wait for work, and waiting real time for a
  deadline that the application's clock controls.
- Asserting short wall-clock timings, such as completion within 100 ms; they fail
  under parallel load.
- Retrying a test that fails only under load instead of fixing its timing cause.
- Using EF Core InMemory as evidence for relational behavior.

## Verification

Run SPM-309's `FastTestInfrastructureSamplesTests`: two databases from
`CreateMigratedDatabaseAsync` arrive migrated and do not see each other's rows,
and moving `SampleTestClock` releases a deadline on the application's clock
without waiting. In a consumer, check that a full run starts one container per
provider and migrates once. A test project above one to two minutes, or a single
test above a few seconds, is a finding: profile container start, migrations, host
start and waits before adding tests to it.

## Separate reusable test helpers from library tests

Use the packable NewHeap .Test projects only as reusable test support for consumers, and keep NewHeap library regression tests in separate non-packable .Tests projects.

## Preferred approach

Reference `NewHeap.Platform.Common.Test` from a consumer test project for DI
contexts, `TaskResult` assertions, and NSubstitute predicate helpers. Add
`NewHeap.Platform.AspNet.Common.Test` for the in-memory DbContext test context
and automatic repository registration. The SampleProjectManagement tests for
SPM-173 through SPM-176 are the executable examples.

Keep the test framework version consumer-owned. The reusable packages do not
reference or flow xUnit compile/runtime assets into consumer test projects, so
a consumer can select its supported xUnit version without duplicate test
attributes. `NhTestingContextFixture<TContext>` exposes lifecycle methods but
does not implement a version-specific xUnit interface; consumers that need an
xUnit class fixture add a small version-specific adapter in their own test
project, as demonstrated by SPM-173. Resolve contexts and application services
from the validated DI provider instead of manually constructing NewHeap
repositories.

Keep the packable `NewHeap.Platform.*.Test` projects limited to public, reusable
fixtures, contexts, factories, and assertions. Put NewHeap's own `[Fact]` and
`[Theory]` regression tests under `src/Back-end/Tests` in a `*.Tests` project
with `IsPackable=false` and `IsTestProject=true`. CI still runs the library
tests, but they never become part of a consumer package.

## Avoid

- Adding library regression tests to a packable `.Test` helper project.
- Referencing an internal `NewHeap.Platform.*.Tests` project from a consumer.
- Relying on a transitive test-framework dependency instead of declaring the
  consumer's chosen runner and test framework explicitly.
- Using EF Core InMemory as evidence for query translation, migrations,
  relational constraints, transactions, or provider-specific behavior.
- Expecting the complete password sign-in on InMemory. Its claims and access
  token (`INhAuthenticationService.CreateToken`) load there, but the session
  also stores a refresh token and deletes expired ones with
  `ExecuteDeleteAsync`, which InMemory cannot run; prove sign-in, division
  claims and their lockout days on SQL Server and PostgreSQL.
- Publishing test-runner, coverage, or browser dependencies when no public
  helper API depends on them.

## Verification

Run the relevant non-packable `*.Tests` project and the consumer test project.
Verify that the helper assemblies contain no `[Fact]` or `[Theory]` methods and
that only the `.Test` helper projects appear as NuGet packages in the release
manifest. For relational behavior, run the required SQL Server and PostgreSQL
tests in addition to any in-memory unit tests.
